https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: The hedge fund titans who made millions during Covid market turmoil
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: Some high-profile financiers sailed through the pandemic, writes Jim Armitage. Others didn’t, but still earned themselves millions
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Howard’s way to £56mAlan Howard, the billionaire financier and Conservative Party donor, emerged last week as one of London’s best-paid hedge fund managers, having scooped a cool £55.8 million at his Brevan Howard fund.
The immensely private investor, 58, has seen his fund post double-digit percentage gains in two of the past three years, with assets under management rebounding to about $16 billion (£12 billion) after sinking to $6 billion in 2018. Reports suggest his bets on bonds, currencies and interest rates paid off as the coronavirus roiled the financial markets.
Brevan Howard has now started implementing plans to expand its investments in crypto and other digital assets, following Goldman Sachs, Marshall Wace, Renaissance Capital and others. Howard stepped back as chief executive in 2019 to be replaced by risk officer Aron Landy, but is still thought to be the “highest paid member” of the firm as detailed in the accounts.
Rokos rakes in £509m from Covid bets If you thought Howard’s pay was hefty, it is dwarfed by that of Chris Rokos, his Brevan Howard co-founder who quit to set up his own fund, reportedly because of a dispute over pay. He has no such money worries now: after a stellar performance during the early months of the Covid crisis, he took home £509.4 million from the £914.7 million profit pot at his Rokos Capital Management fund, according to accounts for the year to March 2021.
Rokos, 51, was state educated in London before winning a scholarship to Eton and then achieving a first at Pembroke College, Oxford.
Rokos Capital Management’s 44 per cent investment gains in 2020 did not continue into 2021, when his bets on short-dated bonds suffered from a sell-off in the market. Despite that, Rokos’s performance during the pandemic meant he easily raised $1 billion from investors in a recent fundraising.
Horror show for HintzeSir Michael Hintze, the Australian-born Conservative Party donor, had an annus horribilis in 2020: his funds investing in companies’ credit were hit badly as Covid smashed into his hard-to-hedge exposures.
The ABS and Directional Opportunities funds of his asset manager CQS were the worst hit, having taken bets on the creditworthiness of oil companies and airlines such as Lufthansa (pictured). Overall, profits available to be distributed to CQS partners more than halved to £45.8 million. Hintze, 68, had to rub by on £28.2 million, down on £31.6 million the year before.
The other 30-odd members of the partnership averaged £1.5 million, down from £2.56 million. A restructuring in 2020 cut about 50 staff. Questions had already been raised about the firm, even before Covid, due to the departure of former London Stock Exchange boss Xavier Rolet.
Business has picked up lately with assets under management swelling.
BlueCrest runs into troubleBlueCrest Capital Management, set up by Lancashire-born billionaire Mike Platt, 53, hit the headlines just before Christmas when it was fined more than £40 million by the Financial Conduct Authority.
The watchdog accused the company of failing to manage a conflict of interest between external investors and its own fund managers back in 2015. BlueCrest is appealing.
The firm switched from being a hedge fund investing other people’s money to a family office in 2016, but its performance is still keenly watched.
Last year, it set aside £74 million of profit for its 58 members, including £40.4 million to a corporate member called Special Capital controlled by BlueCrest chief executive Peter Cox and Jersey-based solicitor Robert Heaselgrave.
Pandemic takes toll on HohnThe Children’s Investment Fund, Sir Chris Hohn’s, above, hedge fund, made a hefty $341 million (£249 million) profit last year, but that was down on the previous year’s $670 million after a steep fall in performance fees as Covid hit its investments. The dividend Hohn paid himself also fell sharply — by more than two-thirds to $153 million. In fairness, the previous year had been “exceptional”, the company said.
Hohn is known as a particularly aggressive activist investor, taking stakes in companies and demanding management change strategy.
He donates much of TCI’s profits to charity, primarily The Children’s Investment Fund Foundation, which he gifted $71.9 million last year. A further $11.9 million went to the CH Foundation. A committed environmentalist, he is also Extinction Rebellion’s biggest donor.
Hohn, 55, is the son of a Jamaican car mechanic.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Outcry over energy-sucking Facebook data centre that threatens Dutch green targets
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Facebook has been hit by an outcry over plans to build a giant data centre in the Netherlands that will use as much electricity as the nation’s railway system or a major city.
Meta, the social media giant’s parent company, says it has stipulated that the 166-hectare (410-acre) complex at Zeewolde must be run from renewable power sources. However, the plan is rapidly becoming the biggest headache for a new, fragile coalition government because its sheer scale threatens the nation’s climate change targets.
The server farm for content on Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp will consume 1,380 gigawatt hours of energy a year, representing about 10 per cent of Dutch wind energy production. The plan would mean the Netherlands would have to rejig climate change targets, which it is already struggling with.
“We find it irresponsible to saddle a future generation with this energy issue,” said Ben Sonneveld of the Leefbaar, or “Liveable”, Zeewolde pressure group, which has eight elected councillors.
“For the energy transition, this means that there will be considerable demand,” Frans Rooijers, director of the environmental research agency CE Delft, said. “Those targets must now be increased to prevent the extra electricity demand from being produced by gas and coal-fired power stations.”
The Netherlands has already been hit by controversies over data centres after a row over a Microsoft facility at Wieringermeer taking the bulk of local electricity produced by 82 wind turbines.
Even before the Facebook project, data storage and transmission consumed some 3 per cent of the Netherlands’ electricity, a share that is expected to rise to more than 10 per cent by 2030.
The issue is fast becoming a problem across Europe. In Denmark, where Meta has a major data centre, 15 per cent of national energy production will be needed to power servers by the end of decade. In Ireland, which is a hub for American tech companies, the national energy provider EirGrid has warned that data centres will suck up almost 30 per cent of the country’s electricity by 2028.
Zeewolde council fought off the protests to approve the complex just before Christmas. The Dutch Senate, the country’s upper house of parliament, has since challenged the decision, meaning the government must make a final ruling.
It has polarised local politics with farmers, concerned at the loss of prime agricultural land, accusing the municipality of “dancing to the tune of ‘big monopolists’ ”.
Jaap Lodders, a farming representative, accused councillors of being “led by empty promises and commitments that cannot be substantiated” rather than the “actual local consequences”.
Guus Dix, a local Extinction Rebellion activist, accused the social media company’s plan of threatening to derail Dutch climate change policies. “The arrival of this data centre will have a huge impact on the energy system in the Netherlands. Moreover, Facebook is not a nice company,” he said.
Mark Rutte, the Dutch prime minister, has promised that stricter rules will be introduced for data centres but has also pledged to encourage more foreign investment in the Netherlands. He will have to take the final decision on the Meta centre as some of it is to be built on government land.
Stijn Grove, the managing director of Dutch Data Centre Association, has accused opponents of the new facility of hypocrisy. “The objections are also hypocritical. As if those data centres are not necessary. Everyone uses them, but we don’t want them in our country?” he said.
Hendrik Visser, a Zeewolde councillor and supporter of the project, said such facilities were “simply necessary” in the 21st century. “They have to go somewhere, and it’s probably not imprudent to build them here in western Europe, under our laws,” he said.
The Zeewolde centre will provide some 400 jobs as well as economic growth and significant revenues to the local authorities. Gerrit Jan Gorter, the mayor of Zeewolde, has accused opponents of the project of being taken in by “fake news” and “myths” over energy usage. “People still believe what’s in the newspaper,” he said.
